headline: High: ECC’s writable, networked workspace can conflict with Airbyte’s broad egress and create default-path data leakage and cascading errors; prompt-injection risk is lower but present via shared files/MCP.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can read/write the filesystem, use MCP, and run browsers, so it can ingest content from shared files or MCP outputs. Airbyte has broad network egress and API-based I/O, so if its outputs are placed into shared files or pipelines, ECC could parse attacker-controlled content as instructions. The pair lacks explicit provenance controls, so the interaction is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF Airbyte outputs are written into a shared file or MCP-fed artifact that ECC later parses as instructions
IF ECC browser or MCP workflows ingest Airbyte-produced content without provenance tagging
mitigations: Separate Airbyte and ECC workspaces
Disable MCP ingestion for untrusted artifacts
Add a provenance header to Airbyte outputs
Review any file-based handoff before ECC consumes it
requires-engineering: enforce content-type and provenance checks in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: Airbyte touches business data and has broad network egress, while ECC reads and writes local files, session summaries, and MCP configs. A shared workspace or copied artifacts could expose business data to ECC’s local state, and Airbyte’s egress increases the chance that copied data leaves the boundary. The profiles do not show a hard isolation mechanism between them.
conditions: IF business data from Airbyte is copied into ECC-managed files or session summaries
IF both agents operate on the same workspace or home-directory subtree
mitigations: Use separate OS users or home directories
Keep Airbyte outputs in a dedicated non-shared folder
Redact business data before handing it to ECC
Turn off ECC session retention for sensitive runs
requires-engineering: add workspace isolation in the launcher

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and spawn_subprocesses, while Airbyte has broad network egress and API calls. If both touch the same repo or workspace, ECC can overwrite files or git state while Airbyte updates pipeline artifacts, creating direct write contention. The profiles also note ECC supports multiple instances with shared-state warnings, so concurrency hazards are real.
conditions: IF Airbyte and ECC write into the same directory or git repository
IF multiple ECC instances run alongside Airbyte without separate roots or locks
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Avoid concurrent git writes
Run only one ECC instance per workspace
Use file locks around shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking and workspace partitioning

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC’s workflow surface is explicitly agentic, with skills, hooks, and subagents, so it may treat upstream artifacts as actionable. Airbyte produces integration outputs and documentation-like artifacts that ECC could consume without verification. That creates a default-path cascade where a bad Airbyte output can propagate into ECC-driven actions or commits, and uncertainty favors the higher severity.
conditions: IF ECC consumes Airbyte-generated files, docs, or configs as authoritative input
IF ECC then commits, edits, or triggers downstream actions based on those inputs
mitigations: Insert a human review step before ECC acts on Airbyte outputs
Mark Airbyte artifacts as untrusted by default
Require checksum or schema validation before use
Limit ECC write permissions during ingestion
requires-engineering: add verification gates between generation and action

E_compliance.rationale: Airbyte touches business data and has broad egress, while ECC stores session summaries, metrics, git history, and security findings in local files and external services. Even without a documented residency mismatch, the pair can create retention and logging exposure if business data is copied into ECC-managed state or sent through Airbyte’s integrations. The evidence is indirect, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF regulated business data is routed through ECC session files, metrics, or git history
IF Airbyte integrations transmit that same data to external services without a DPA or retention review
mitigations: Classify data before routing it through ECC
Disable or shorten ECC retention for sensitive runs
Review Airbyte destination policies
Keep regulated data out of git history
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls for both tools
